english: The Flight of the Dragons

A hundred years ago, the world called my forefather Aenar a fool. Lord Aenar Targaryen, a lesser dragonlord of mighty Valyria, who sold his estates and moved his whole house - wives, children, dragons and all - to a bleak smoking rock at the western edge of the world, on no better counsel than the dreams of his daughter. Twelve years later, the Fourteen Flames tore Valyria apart in a single day and night, and the greatest civilization the world has known drowned in fire and salt water. Daenys the Dreamer had seen truly. Of all the dragonlords of the Freehold, only we endured. We are the last.

For a hundred years since - the century the world remembers as one long letting of blood - the daughters of Valyria have torn at each other over the corpse of their mother. I have had my taste of those wars: when Pentos and Tyrosh sought the aid of the young Lord of Dragonstone against the grasping Volantenes, I flew Balerion east, burned a war fleet to the waterline, and came home. The lords magister feasted me and begged me to stay. I would not. There is nothing in the east but old ashes quarreling over older ashes.

#bold It is the west that has always called to me. It called to Aenar across a hundred years - and now, at last, I understand why.#!
The west calls.
The Painted Table

Years ago I commanded the carpenters of Dragonstone to carve me a table. They thought their lord mad by the time it was done - fifty feet long, five-and-twenty wide at its broadest, hewn from a single mighty block and painted, every inch, in the likeness of Westeros. Every river and bay, every mountain range and ruined ringfort, every castle and town and holdfast from Oldtown to the Wall, set down exactly - my painters worked from the charts of a hundred traders and the accounts of a thousand travelers.

One thing, and one thing only, I forbade them to paint: borders. Wander the table's length and you will find no line where the stormlands end and the Reach begins, no seam dividing the kingdoms the Andals carved out of one another. From the raised seat at Dragonstone's place - where I sit now, with the brazier crackling behind me and my sisters at either hand - a man sees the truth those lines were drawn to hide.

#bold It was never seven kingdoms. It is one land. It wants only one king.#!
One land. One king.
The Arrogant Stag

Harren the Black's monstrous castle by the Gods Eye nears completion at last, and forty years of the riverlands' misery with it. A man who has spent a lifetime building the greatest fortress in the world does not intend to sit quietly in it; all Westeros whispers that Harren looks about for new conquests - and none whisper more anxiously than his neighbor the Storm King.

So Argilac Durrandon, grown old and, for the first time in his proud life, afraid, sent his offer across the water: an alliance against Harren, sealed with the hand of his daughter Argella - and a dowry of lands along the Blackwater to stand as a buffer between stag and kraken. Lands, be it noted, that Harren holds and Argilac does not; the old man offered me another king's ground. I declined the lady with courtesy - the blood of the dragon does not want for wives; I have two, my sisters, wed as Valyria always wed. In her place I offered the hand of Orys Baratheon, my dearest friend and, the whispers say, my brother - and asked lands within Argilac's actual gift as the dowry.

His answer arrived today, in a box. The hands of my envoy, salted like pork. And a message: #italic 'These are the only hands you shall receive.'#!

#bold The Arrogant, they call him. He has earned the name today - and he will learn the price of it.#!
Argilac will lose more than hands for this.
The Lord of Dragonstone

The box sits open on the Painted Table. My envoy will live, the maester says. He will never hold a sword again.

I have been patient. For years the kings of Westeros have sent their ravens to Dragonstone - seeking my dragons for their wars, my fleet for their quarrels, my house for their daughters - as though the blood of the dragon were a sellsword company to be hired, flattered, and dismissed. Argilac's insult is only the last and grossest of a hundred. They see a petty lord on a barren rock. They have forgotten what came out of Valyria and what the Doom could not kill.

I am done with the courtesies of petty lords and false kings. Of all the houses of Old Valyria, only mine came through the Doom with its dragons, and no one else under the sun has any. They have taken my patience for weakness - every one of them.

#bold No longer. Westeros will be mine.#!
#S We answer with fire and blood. #!
The Dragon Flies West

I have called my banners and taken counsel - with my sisters, with Orys, with the lords of the narrow sea. The Velaryons and Celtigars, kin to my house and Valyrian as we are, were mine before I finished speaking; Lord Bar Emmon of Sharp Point and Lord Massey of Stonedance knelt the same hour. Small lords, the kings of Westeros would say. The first lords of a new realm, say I.

Then I sent the ravens - one to every king and great lord in Westeros, each bearing the same words. That from this day there is one king in Westeros. That those who bend the knee to Aegon of House Targaryen shall keep their lands and titles, diminished in nothing but their crowns. And that those who take up arms against him shall be thrown down, humbled, and destroyed.

The maesters will note that I addressed no kingdoms, acknowledged no borders, treated the seven crowns as seven vanities. That was no oversight. I have stood at the Painted Table; I know what Westeros is, even if Westeros does not yet know it itself.

#bold Every hall from Sunspear to Winterfell will read it: the dragon does not ask twice.#!
There is only one king in Westeros.
The Toad and the Hawk Reply

The ravens return, and two answers among them want remembering.

From Sunspear writes Meria Martell, Princess of Dorne - eighty years old, blind, immense, and cunning as ever her enemies feared: the Yellow Toad offers me alliance against Argilac the Storm King. Alliance. She will fight beside me, share the spoils with me - and yield me nothing. From the Eyrie writes Sharra Arryn, regent of the Vale for her boy Ronnel, with a subtler snare: an alliance sealed with her own hand in marriage - she sends a portrait, and word that she was once called the Flower of the Mountain - provided only that I name her son my heir. She covets the east bank of the Green Fork, and would have my dragons win it from Harren for her.

I have refused them both, the toad and the hawk alike, and in the same words: I did not send my ravens seeking allies. I sent them seeking subjects. There is no place in what is coming for kings and queens who would treat with me as equals - for I have no equals in Westeros.

#bold They may keep their crowns a little longer. I shall come for them in due course - and I will come beneath a banner all the world shall learn.#!
I seek subjects, not allies.
The Three Heads of the Dragon

The dragonlords of old Valyria kept no banners. The Freehold flew no sigils to war; a dragon overhead was herald enough. But I do not mean to rule Valyria - I mean to rule Westeros, and Westeros reads the world through its banners: direwolf and kraken, lion and stag, falcon and sun-and-spear.

So let them have one to remember. Visenya has overseen the work herself: a field black as Balerion's wings, and upon it a dragon red as flame, #bold three-headed#! - one head for me, one for each of my sister-queens, for it is the three of us together who will do this thing. When the maesters of far-off ages write of how the Seven Kingdoms became one, this is the banner that will fly over every page.

#bold Fire and blood, on black and red. It will be sewn on every sail. #!
One head for each of us. Raise it over Dragonstone.
A Claim Cast Across Westeros

A raven has crossed the Gods Eye bearing Aegon Targaryen's demand: every king in Westeros is to surrender his crown and name the Lord of Dragonstone his sovereign. He offers peace to those who kneel and fire to those who refuse.

The boy has three dragons, but I have Harrenhal—the greatest fortress ever raised, with walls no army can breach and towers no flame can threaten. Aegon may come and dash himself against the monument I spent forty years building.

#bold Stone does not burn, and Harren the Black does not kneel.#!

A raven from Dragonstone has reached Winterfell. Aegon Targaryen styles himself king of all Westeros and commands every crowned head to lay down his crown. Those who submit may keep their lands; those who resist are promised fire and blood.

The North has followed Stark kings since the Long Night. No southern conqueror has ever crossed the Neck and ruled us, yet no southern conqueror ever came astride Balerion, with Vhagar and Meraxes at either wing. Soon I must call the banners and decide what an ancient crown is worth in northern lives.

#bold The North remembers its kings. The dragon will learn that.#!

Aegon Targaryen's raven has flown as far as Sunspear. The dragonlord commands me to yield my crown, bend my knee, and acknowledge him as king of all Westeros. Submission will bring peace, he says; refusal will bring dragonfire.

The other kings may count their walls and armies. Dorne has survived greater powers by offering neither battle nor surrender, only empty roads, poisoned wells, and sands that swallow invaders whole. Dragons may burn what they can find. We shall give them precious little to find.

#bold Unbowed, Unbent, Unbroken. That is my answer.#!

Aegon Targaryen has sent his terms to Casterly Rock. He claims all Westeros as one realm beneath one king and bids me exchange the crown of the Rock for his peace. If I refuse, the raven warns, he will answer with Balerion, Vhagar, and Meraxes.

The Westerlands are rich enough to arm hosts beyond counting, and Mern Gardener commands the greatest strength in the Reach. Together our banners could cover the earth from horizon to horizon. Yet the Targaryens mean to fight from the sky. Gold has purchased every weapon known to men; now it must purchase an answer to dragons.

#bold The lion has not ruled the Rock for six thousand years merely to become a dragon's cat.#!

The Lord of Dragonstone has sent a raven to Highgarden declaring himself king of all Westeros. Aegon Targaryen offers mercy if I surrender the green crown and threatens fire if I do not. Three dragons, he believes, outweigh the oldest dynasty and greatest host in the realm.

Every field of the Reach can yield another company of spears. Loren Lannister shares my danger, and the might of Highgarden joined to the gold of Casterly Rock will make an army such as Westeros has never seen. The dragonlord has wings, but he must still take and hold a continent.

#bold House Gardener has flourished since the dawn of kings. I will not be its last bloom.#!

Another message has come from the boy on Dragonstone. After answering my daughter's hand with the offer of his bastard brother, Aegon Targaryen now demands my crown as well. He names himself king of all Westeros and promises fire to every ruler who will not kneel.

I have broken Dornish hosts, slain kings, and defended these stormlands since before Aegon first sat a saddle. His beasts are terrible, but storms have cast down prouder things than dragons, and Storm's End was raised to defy the fury of the gods themselves.

#bold He knows where to find me. The last Storm King still has one war left in him.#!

A raven has come from the dragonlord. Mother read it twice and then shut herself in council with the lords of the Vale. Aegon Targaryen says all Westeros is one kingdom now, and every king must give him his crown or face his three dragons.

They say no army can pass the Bloody Gate and no castle is safer than the Eyrie. But dragons do not climb roads. Balerion is large enough to swallow a horse, Vhagar is nearly as fierce, and Meraxes has golden eyes. Everyone looks afraid when they think I am not watching.

#bold I am King of Mountain and Vale. Surely even a dragon must ask before taking my crown.#!

Ravens now carry Aegon Targaryen's proclamation to every court in Westeros: the Lord of Dragonstone claims the whole continent and names himself its king. Many laugh at the presumption, but wiser rulers remember the doom that dragons once brought to armies and cities. \n \nAegon does not come alone. Visenya rides Vhagar, Rhaenys rides Meraxes, and Balerion the Black Dread answers to Aegon himself. Soon the Seven Kingdoms will learn whether ancient crowns can withstand the last power of Valyria.
Our ancient crowns will not yield so easily.
What is dead may never die—and Harrenhal shall never fall.
Winter is coming, even for dragons.
Unbowed, Unbent, Unbroken.
The lion will answer with claws.
The Green Hand shall not wither before dragonfire.
Ours is the Fury. Come, dragon.
As High as Honor—higher even than dragons.
The Last Stone

Forty years. Forty years of the rivers' timber and the rivers' gold and the rivers' backs bent to my quarries, and today the masons set the last stone of Harrenhal. Five towers to shame the mountains, walls no engine built by man could trouble, halls that could stable armies. No castle in all the world has ever matched it. None ever will.

And on this same day, a raven from Dragonstone. The Valyrian salt-lordling bids me kneel — me, whose line has worn crowns since before his precious freehold was ash — or be destroyed.

The gods below have a sense of humour after all. He may come and look upon what I have built. Valyria has been dead for a hundred years. I will not kneel to what is left of it, and if he brings it to my gates, he will find them shut.
Come, dragon, and learn what stone means.
The Box of Hands

The dragonlord's envoy stood beneath Durran Godsgrief's roof and delivered his master's answer as though it were some great courtesy. I had offered Aegon Targaryen my daughter's hand and lands that Harren Hoare has no right to hold, enough to make common cause between two kings against a common enemy. The heathen refused Argella for himself. Instead he offered me Orys, his baseborn half-brother, and presumed to name still more lands besides.

There are insults a king may swallow for the good of his realm. This was not one of them.

The envoy leaves Storm's End with Aegon's answer returned to him in a cedar box. His hands are inside it. If Orys Waters desires something of mine badly enough to reach for it, he may begin with those.

Aegon may sit upon his smoking rock with his sister-wives and mistake restraint for weakness if it pleases him. The Storm Kings were fighting ironmen, Dornishmen, and worse before Valyria was ash, and I have not survived this long by fearing every foreign lord with a strange name and a monstrous beast beneath him. If the dragon wants war, by the Seven, he shall learn why my house has kept these lands for a thousand years.

#bold The storm has given its answer. Dragonstone may make what it will of it.#!
The storm answers with fury.
King's Landing

Our ships are drawn up where the Blackwater Rush meets the bay, and I chose the place with care: the land is claimed by both Argilac the Arrogant and Harren the Black, which is to say defended by neither. The two of them can quarrel over whose problem I am. Three hills rise north of the river: a high hill, a wooded hill away to the north, and a lower one nearer the water. No one has yet troubled to give them names. That will change.

On the high hill my men are already raising a fort of earth and timber, while my sisters attend to our first task - the lords of the shore. Rhaenys is flying Meraxes to Rosby, and Visenya is taking Vhagar to Stokeworth. Both lords will kneel to their king, or face dragonflame.

#bold A fort of logs today; a city, one day. The maesters may argue over its name. #!
Here the conquest takes root.
The Dragon at the Blackwater

The Targaryen has put ashore at the mouth of the Blackwater and thrown up a ditch and a timber palisade on the high hill. My land, as it happens — though the quarrelsome little lords of that shore forget whose peace they keep whenever it suits them.

He hopes to sting me into rushing down to meet him, no doubt. Why would I? Every day he sits in his mud fort, my walls stand just as high. He can bleed himself on Darklyn and Mooton and the Storm King's pride first.

When he has worn his little host to rags, he may come and break what remains of it against Harrenhal.
The shore lords can blunt him first.
The Dragon Comes Ashore

Word from the Blackwater: the Targaryen has landed at the river's mouth, on the three hills where the fisherfolk beach their boats. A few thousand men, some ships, and the three beasts of Dragonstone.

The mouth of the Blackwater is Harren's land — let the old squid dig him out, or lose the rivers trying. Both would suit me. Whichever of them bleeds first, the Stormlands watch, and arm, and wait.

Storms have broken on these lands since Durran defied the gods themselves. A lizard with wings does not frighten me.
The dragon and the squid can tear at each other.
The First to Kneel

My sisters return before the week is out, and behind them come the first oaths.

Rhaenys found Rosby's gates open. The old lord watched Meraxes circle his towers once, twice, and had his banners struck before she finished the third pass; he met her in his own yard, knelt on the cobbles, and offered bread, salt, and homage without a single bolt loosed. His seat lies a short ride from our three hills, his lands run with the chalk road toward Duskendale, and his house is old enough to remember when kings were smaller things. He strikes me as a man who means to survive whatever comes next. I can use such men.

Stokeworth cost a little more. Visenya came down over their keep, and their crossbowmen - braver than their lord, or perhaps only worse informed - loosed a volley at her. Vhagar answered with a single breath. The roofs of the keep took flame, and the same crossbowmen spent the evening hauling water while their lord waved a peace banner from the walls. Rich farms, full granaries, and a house that will spend the next hundred years insisting it was faithful from the first. The scorched rafters will only make the tale better.

Two oaths, then, and the whole shore watching: Hayford, Rook's Rest, the Antlers, a dozen petty lords weighing dragons against the old crowns. Only from Duskendale and Maidenpool, where the Darklyns and the Mootons sit, has there come no word at all.

#bold The silence to the north has a sound I know. It is the sound of swords being counted.#!
Bread and salt for the faithful.
The Aegonfort

The fort is finished - or finished enough for a king to sleep in it.

We raised it on the tallest of the three hills, where I first planted the banner: a ring of raw logs and packed earth, a timber hall roofed in thatch and hides, stables, a smithy, a longhouse for the men. There is not a block of dressed stone in the whole of it. Visenya walked the wall once and called it a woodpile waiting for a torch. She is not wrong. It will serve.

From its gate I can see everything I came for: the bay, the river mouth, and the fishing village below swelling day by day into a town of tents and mud lanes - traders, masons, camp followers, septons, every kind of man who can smell a court being born. The smallfolk have already named the hills. This one is Aegon's High Hill now; the wooded one to the north is Rhaenys's, and the one by the water Visenya's. And the town needs no maester to name it. Men simply say they are going to the king's landing.

Balerion suns himself on the slope below the wall, which does more for the fort's defenses than every log in it.

It is well he does. Word comes at dusk that the Darklyns of Duskendale and the Mootons of Maidenpool have called their banners and joined their strength. They mean to come and burn my woodpile.

#bold They are welcome to try. Every king must have a seat, and mine will outgrow the both of theirs.#!
This will do. For a start.
Three Thousand Swords

My outriders have counted them on the road out of Duskendale: three thousand men, with carts, camp followers and levies strung out behind. They march openly and they march slowly, which tells me they expect a battle at the end of it and not a hunt.

I can put fewer than sixteen hundred in the field, and half of those are narrow sea men who fight better from a deck than a ditch.

Neither lord has ever seen a dragon. Their whole plan rests on that, and they do not know it.

#bold They have until the ditch to think better of this.#!
Three thousand men. I have three dragons.
The Aegonfort Stands to Arms

The ditch is dug, the palisade is up, and my sisters do not agree.

Visenya would have us stand behind the timber and make them come to it: men who charge a palisade break on it, she says, and dragons can take them while they are breaking. Rhaenys would rather we rode out and met them on ground I choose, where they will have room to run and nowhere worth running to.

#bold Both counsels end the same way. The difference is only where I stand while it happens.#!
We hold the palisade. They can come to us.
Ride out. I will choose the ground.
Fire on the Rosby Road

They came on at the palisade in good order, and they were still in good order when the sky opened.

Vhagar and Meraxes came out of the sun on either flank. What had been an army was fire and screaming before a man could finish a prayer, and the ditch we dug caught most of those who ran the wrong way.

Lord Darklyn and Lord Mooton burned with their men. Of the host that marched out of Duskendale, the road will not carry a tenth of it home.

#bold The first army raised against me in Westeros is ash. Every hall between here and the Trident will hear of it within the week.#!

I would not fight my first battle in Westeros from behind a ditch. I rode out and took the ground I wanted, with the road at their backs and nothing at all on their flanks.

Then the sky opened. Vhagar and Meraxes came out of the sun on either side of them, and what had been an army was fire and screaming before a man could finish a prayer. My own line never had to hold longer than a moment.

Lord Darklyn and Lord Mooton burned with their men. Of the host that marched out of Duskendale, the road will not carry a tenth of it home.

#bold The first army raised against me in Westeros is ash, and I stood on the field to watch it burn.#!
The first of many.
The Heirs Kneel

They came to the Aegonfort before their dead were buried. Duskendale rode in at first light under a peace banner, Maidenpool followed within the hour, and neither asked for terms.

They knelt in the mud outside a half-built hall, gave up their castles, and asked one thing: their names and their lands. I granted it. Visenya already has men counting what sits in the Duskendale warehouses - it is the busiest port on the narrow sea, and tonight it is mine.

#bold Their fathers would not kneel, so their heirs do. Westeros should see both halves of that.#!
Rise. You keep your names and your lands.
The First Trial

Word of our landing ran up the coast faster than our outriders. Lord Darklyn of Duskendale and Lord Mooton of Maidenpool joined their strength - three thousand men, by the count of our scouts - and marched south to drive us back into the sea that brought us. It was the first true test of this conquest, and it lasted less than a morning.

Orys met them with our vanguard and broke their line; Rhaenys came down upon their rear on Meraxes, and what had been a host became a rout. Both lords lie among the slain. Darklyn's son and Mooton's brother knelt to me on the field, amid their own dead, and did homage for their fathers' halls - and they shall keep them. All Westeros will mark it: those who bend the knee will find me open-handed. Those who take up swords against me will find I keep the swords.

For I have ordered the blades of the fallen gathered, every one, and carried up the high hill to the Aegonfort. I have a purpose for them - and it will want many more swords yet before it is done.

#bold The ground about our landing is secure. Westeros has tested us, and been answered.#!
Gather up their swords.
A Circlet of Valyrian Steel

My sisters would wait no longer. A conqueror who names himself king of all Westeros, Visenya said, ought to look the part before the lords he means to rule - and there are lords enough to witness it now, new-sworn and watching to see what manner of man holds their oaths.

So it was done - though no grand affair: a bare handful of lords stood witness in the timber hall, the new-sworn shore lords and my own captains, with the banners of Darklyn and Mooton hung fresh among my own. Before them I knelt to my elder sister, as our forebears knelt in the shadow of the Fourteen Flames. Visenya set upon my brow a circlet of Valyrian steel, studded with great square-cut rubies - no southron bauble of gold and velvet, but steel, dark and keen as the work of Old Valyria. It is the only crown I mean to wear.

Then Rhaenys' voice rang out over the ranks, and the words she gave them shall be the style of every king of my line that follows after:

#bold Aegon, First of His Name, King of All Westeros, and Shield of His People.#!

The little company took up the cry - a few dozen voices where one day there will be thousands - and somewhere above the clouds, the dragons answered louder than any host could.

#bold Seven kingdoms do not yet know they have a king. They will learn.#!
#S King of All Westeros. #!
The Hand of the King

A crown is a weight, and a king who bears every weight alone will break beneath them. The lords about me understood this before I had worn mine a day - suddenly there was no shortage of counsel at the Aegonfort, nor of counsellors hungry to be seen giving it.

There was never a question of whom I would raise first. Orys has been at my side since we were boys in the yard at Dragonstone, matching blunted swords before either of us could grow a beard. The court whispers that he is my brother, base-born of my father's blood; I have never dignified the whisper with an answer, and never once denied it. It was Orys who broke the lords Darklyn and Mooton on the field that won us our landing. Where the fighting is thickest, there he is; where I am weakest, there he is also.

So before the assembled court I bade him kneel, and named him the first Hand of the King - and the realm would do well to mark the words I gave him, for I meant every one:

#bold My shield, my stalwart, my strong right hand.#!
Rise, my Lord Hand.
North or South

A crown settles nothing; it only promises. Mine promises all of Westeros, and Westeros is held by kings who mean to keep it. In the hall of the Aegonfort my council bends over the maps, and every finger points a different way.

North sits [fab_ac_harrenhal_lord.GetFirstNameNicknamed], King of the Isles and the Rivers, behind the walls of Harrenhal - the monstrous castle his ironmen wrung out of forty years of riverland blood and toil, finished, the singers say, on the very day I stepped ashore. Five towers like the fingers of a grasping hand, walls too high and thick for any siege ladder ever made. [fab_ac_harrenhal_lord.GetFirstName] thinks [fab_ac_harrenhal_lord.GetHerHis] stone will keep [fab_ac_harrenhal_lord.GetHerHim]. The rivermen who built it groan beneath his yoke, and I am told some of their lords would rise for me - if someone gave them cause.

South waits Argilac the Arrogant, the old Storm King, who cut the hands from my envoy and sent them to me in a box. His pride began this war. He is old, but the strength is not gone from him, and unlike [fab_ac_harrenhal_lord.GetFirstName] he will not cower behind walls - the Durrandon will come out to meet me in the open field, storm and all. There would be a certain justice in answering him first.

#bold Two kings, two roads. Either way, the wars for Westeros begin in earnest.#!
Set the host upon the road to Harrenhal.
We will answer Argilac first.
The Host Divides

The war will not wait on carpenters, so this morning I put the host on its roads.

Mine runs northwest, up the Blackwater to the Gods Eye, with Balerion above it. Visenya sails north with Daemon Velaryon and the fleet, to learn what the Vale will pay to keep its peace. Orys holds the rest under arms on the southern marches, with Rhaenys and Meraxes over him. Argilac would not have him for a good-son; he can have him for an enemy.

#bold Three roads and three dragons. Mine ends at Harrenhal.#!
Balerion and I will suffice.
The Battle of the Reeds

They were waiting where the reeds grow tall on the southern shore of the Gods Eye, and they chose their moment well. My column was strung out along the water and the ground gave way under armoured men.

What they had not reckoned on was Balerion already aloft. He came in low over the water, the reeds went up from end to end, and after that it was less a battle than a reckoning.

We hold the field. We also have fewer men than we had this morning, and the maesters will be working until dawn.

#bold This country will cost me blood even where I win. Better to learn it here than at the walls.#!
The field is ours. Press on.
The Wailing Willows

They crossed the Gods Eye in the dark with cloth wrapped round their oars, and they know that water better than my scouts know the shore. The first we knew of them was the willows moving where there was no wind.\n\nThey struck the rear, among the wounded and the baggage, and were gone again before the horns stopped sounding. Smashed carts, burning tents, and more of my men dead than the reeds cost me.
\n\nThe prisoners name the two who led them across: [fab_ac_hoare_son_a.GetFirstName] and [fab_ac_hoare_son_b.GetFirstName] Hoare.
\n\nThe prisoners name the man who led them across: [fab_ac_hoare_son_a.GetFirstName] Hoare.
\n\n#bold They fought like ironborn, and they fought well. I shall remember the willows.#!
Count the dead. Then find me those boats.
Balerion on the Water

Whatever the ironborn know about water, the Gods Eye is a lake, and a lake offers a longship nowhere to hide. They were still out on it at first light, rowing low and heavy with everything they had carried off.\n\nBalerion took them in open water. The boats burned to the waterline, and men in mail do not swim.
\n\n[fab_ac_hoare_son_a.GetFirstName] and [fab_ac_hoare_son_b.GetFirstName] Hoare went out onto that lake last night. Neither came back.
\n\n[fab_ac_hoare_son_a.GetFirstName] Hoare went out onto that lake last night. He did not come back.
\n\n#bold The willows are paid for. Now Harrenhal.#!
Word will reach Harrenhal before I do.

She found it empty. Not taken, not fled in panic - emptied, deliberately, to the last spear and the last sack of grain. In the town beneath the walls only women and children and old men remained, drawing water and tending goats as though a dragon in the market square were no stranger than a dust storm. When my sister asked where their lords and fighting men had gone, they gave her one word, every one of them, courteous and closed as a shut gate:

#bold 'Away.'#!

Harren hid behind stone, and stone melted. Argilac came out to fight, and died. The Dornish mean to hide behind emptiness itself - and emptiness does not burn.

#bold Rhaenys flies on toward Sunspear. If the lords of Dorne will not receive her, their princess shall.#!
To Sunspear, then.
The Yellow Toad

At Sunspear, the ancient seat of House Martell, my sister found the same defiant silence - the winding alleys of the shadow city deserted, the Old Palace unbarred and unguarded. But this castle was not quite empty. In her own hall, alone beneath the spear-and-sun banners, the Princess of Dorne sat waiting for the dragon.

Meria Martell has ruled Dorne for sixty years. She is eighty years of age, very fat, blind, and almost bald, her skin sallow and sagging - the Yellow Toad of Dorne, her enemies named her long ago, and most of those enemies are dust now while she still sits her chair. Neither age nor blindness has dulled her wits by so much as a hair, and she greeted the Queen of Westeros without rising, without fear, and without ceremony.

She offered no defiance of banners or hosts. She offered something harder to answer:

#bold 'I will not fight you, nor will I kneel to you. Dorne has no king. Tell your brother that.'#!
#bold I shall - but we will come again, Princess... #!
#bold ...and the next time, we shall come with fire and blood. #!
Dorne Will Not Kneel

The old princess heard my sister's warning without so much as a flicker. Fire and blood, promised by a Targaryen queen with a dragon on her doorstep - and the Yellow Toad might have been listening to a fishwife complain about the weather. Then she gave her answer, and I suspect the singers will keep it longer than they keep most of what kings say:

#bold 'Your words. Ours are Unbowed, Unbent, Unbroken. You may burn us, my lady ... but you will not bend us, break us, or make us bow. This is Dorne. You are not wanted here. Return at your peril.'#!

Thus queen and princess parted, and Dorne remained unconquered.

An old blind woman alone in an empty castle has done what Harren's stone and Argilac's storm and the iron fist of the Two Kings could not: she has sent a Targaryen home without a submission. I will not pretend the audacity of it does not command a certain respect - nor that it changes anything. Dorne's reckoning is deferred, not forgiven.

#bold The toad keeps her deserts - for now. There is a crown waiting for me in Oldtown first.#!
Queen and princess parted, with Dorne still beyond the Iron Throne.
The Toad Receives a Dragon

They tell me the dragon queen found Vaith just as I arranged it: the castle bare, the granaries carted away, and no soul left in the town but grandmothers and babes with one word to give her. Away. You cannot burn away.

And so she came to Sunspear, as I knew she must, and found me waiting alone in my own hall. I am eighty years old, blind, fat and nearly bald — my enemies named me the Yellow Toad half a century ago, and I have buried nearly all of them since. A dragon on my doorstep does not hurry my pulse.

I told her plainly: I will not fight you, nor will I kneel to you. Dorne has no king. Tell your brother that.

She promised to come again with fire and blood. Their little words. I gave her ours — unbowed, unbent, unbroken — and sent her home to her brother with nothing. The kings of grass and river may kneel. This is Dorne.
Queen and princess parted, and Dorne still bowed to no one.
My Mother's Answer, and Mine

The dragon queen crossed the Red Mountains the only way that costs Dorne nothing — over them — and found Vaith emptied to the last spear, exactly as my mother planned it before the gods took her. The Yellow Toad is gone, but her design outlives her, and I have not moved a stone of it.

So Rhaenys Targaryen came at last to Sunspear, and found not the old woman she had prepared her courtesies for, but me, alone in the hall my mother sat for sixty years.

I gave her the answer I inherited along with the chair. I will not fight her; there is nothing here for her dragon to fight. I will not kneel to her; Dorne has no king to be conquered. She promised fire and blood, as her house does. I gave her our words back — unbowed, unbent, unbroken — and let the empty sands say the rest.

Rhaenys Comes Home

Meraxes has come home, and my sister with her - empty-handed for the first time in this conquest. She is not accustomed to it. Neither am I.

We have talked long into the night of what a Dornish war would mean, and the truth sits ill with both of us. There is no host to break there, no proud king to meet me in the field, no castle whose burning would end it - only sand, thirst, empty keeps, and spears that strike from the rocks and are gone. Dragons win battles; Dorne offers none. To conquer the deserts would cost me years and legions, and the realm I have just stitched together is too new for either.

So Dorne keeps its sands, and the old woman keeps her chair - for now. No one should mistake patience for pardon.

#bold South and west, then, to the one great gate that has yet to open: Oldtown, the High Septon, and the Hightower. It is time the Faith met the dragon.#!
Dorne can wait. Oldtown cannot.
The Beacon of Oldtown

The Hightower rises above the horizon long before Oldtown's walls come into view, its beacon a pale flame against the southern sky. Beneath it lies the greatest city in Westeros: the Citadel and its grey scholars, the Starry Sept and the Father of the Faithful, wharves crowded with half the wealth of the realm, and more souls than some kingdoms can boast.

The High Septon has spent seven days and seven nights in prayer. Word carried from the city says the Crone showed him Oldtown consumed by dragonfire should the Hightowers resist me. Yet visions do not open gates, and holy counsel does not always master a proud lord.

My host advances along the roseroad beneath the three-headed dragon. Soon the walls sharpen through the morning haze, and the beacon atop the Hightower changes before my eyes.

#bold Now shall I learn whether Oldtown has heeded the Crone's lamp. #!
The dragon flies above open gates. Oldtown has chosen wisely.
The beacon burns green. Oldtown has called its banners.
The Beacon Burns Green

Green fire blazes from the crown of the Hightower.

The gates are barred. A great chain closes the Honeywine, and every bell in Oldtown calls men not to prayer, but to arms. From the orchards and villages beyond the walls come the banners of House Hightower's sworn swords, answering the green flame above their city. The High Septon counselled submission; pride has answered in his stead.

My captains warn that even a short siege will cost gold, men, and time. Oldtown's walls are strong, but stone has failed before me from Harrenhal to the Eyrie, and no wall can close the sky.

#bold The Crone showed them fire. Lord Hightower has chosen to look upon it with his own eyes. #!
Close every road and raise the dragons. Oldtown will open its gates.
The Chain Is Broken

It is finished. The banners of the Honeywine are scattered, the harbour is his, and the three-headed dragon flies from the Hightower where the beacon-flame burns. His beasts circle the tower as I write — slowly, without haste, the way a victor circles.

We wagered ten thousand years of the Hightower's keeping against an old man's vision of fire, and the vision has collected its debt. My sword is surrendered, my knee is bent. That the city was not burned outright is a mercy I did not earn.

His High Holiness — who counselled submission from the first — is to crown the conqueror in the Starry Sept in three days' time. The gods forgive us. The Crone did try to light the way.
Gods, forgive our pride.
Seven Oils Among Ashes

The seven oils are still wet upon my brow when I rise.

Above me there is no crystal dome to catch the morning light. Shards of it lie melted among the blackened stones, and the faces of the Seven stare down from cracked alcoves through veils of smoke. The High Septon found the holy oils beneath a fallen altar. He anointed me where the Starry Sept once stood whole, his hands steady though ash clung to his robes.

Beyond the ruin, Oldtown is silent. No fathers lift their children to see Balerion. No cheering follows my crown through the streets. The Hightower's beacon burns red once more, but beneath it the three-headed dragon flies above broken gates.

I have the blessing of the Faith and the submission of the city, as I came to claim. Yet the oldest sept in Westeros is a smoking shell, the Honeywine is choked with wreckage, and every godly lord in my new-made realm will remember the price of this anointing.

#bold A realm may be hammered into one upon an anvil of stone. It does not follow that the stone will forgive the hammer. #!
The ashes bear witness. I am anointed king.
The Hightower Yields

The greatest city in Westeros did not make me break a single lance for it. As my host came within sight of the Hightower's flame, we found the gates of Oldtown standing open - and Lord Manfred Hightower waiting on the road to offer me his sword, his city, and his oath.

The why of it is a stranger tale than the walls themselves. When word of my landing first reached Oldtown, the High Septon shut himself within the Starry Sept for seven days and seven nights, fasting on bread and water, praying at one altar after the next. On the seventh day, he emerged to declare that the Crone had raised her golden lamp and shown him the path ahead: if Oldtown took up arms against the dragon, Oldtown would burn - the Hightower, the Citadel, and the Starry Sept cast down and destroyed. Lord Manfred is a cautious and a godly man - one son sworn to the Warrior's Sons, another lately a septon - and he heard his Father of the Faithful. Not one man of Oldtown burned on the Field of Fire, though the Hightowers were sworn to Highgarden of old.

So the lord knelt on the road before me and Balerion both, and made his offers - and one offer more: the hand of his youngest daughter. I declined her with every courtesy. A man with two queens does well not to collect a third.

#bold And within the city, they say, His High Holiness is waiting for me. The gods of the Seven wish to crown what the sword has already won.#!
The Crone lit her lamp in good time, my lord. Rise.
The Coronation of Aegon I Targaryen

Three days after the gates of Oldtown opened to me, I knelt beneath the dome of the Starry Sept - the black marble heart of the Faith itself - and His High Holiness anointed my brow with the seven oils, set a crown upon my head, and proclaimed me before gods and men:

#bold Aegon of House Targaryen, the First of His Name, King of the Andals, the Rhoynar, and the First Men, Lord of the Seven Kingdoms, and Protector of the Realm.#!

Seven Kingdoms, His High Holiness said - though Dorne remains unbowed. The style can stand as a promise.

A bare handful of lords stood witness when Visenya first crowned me at the Aegonfort; hundreds filled the Starry Sept today, and among them the maesters and archmaesters of the Citadel in their rings and masks and robes. The grey scribes record what the grey scribes witness - I do not doubt that when the histories are written, it is this day, and not the crowning by the Blackwater, that they will fix as the first of my reign. So be it. A king can be crowned twice; a realm is only forged once.

#bold Thus are the Seven Kingdoms of Westeros hammered into one realm - by my will, my sisters' fire, and now the blessing of the gods the most of my subjects hold most dear.#!
Seven oils, one realm, one king.
I accept the crown - but the gods of Valyria keep my house.
The Dragon in the Streets

The Starry Sept gave me a crown; the streets of Oldtown gave me something rarer.

When the rites were done, I did not return to my host in a litter or beneath a canopy, as the septons no doubt expected of an anointed king. I mounted Balerion in the sept's own square and rode him through the city at a walk - down the winding cobbled streets, past the guildhalls and the wharves, beneath the shadow of the Hightower itself, his wings folded and his black scales shining, my crown still on my brow.

Tens of thousands came out to see it. They packed the streets and the rooftops and hung from the windows, fathers lifting children onto their shoulders to look upon the Black Dread - the greatest beast in the world, walking their streets tame as a palfrey with their new king upon his back. There were screams at first. Then cheering, wave upon wave of it, rolling ahead of us from street to street until the whole city roared.

Fear brought Westeros to its knees. But fear rusts, and crowns won by fear alone rust with it. What Oldtown saw today it will tell for three generations: not the dragon that burns, but the dragon that need not.

#bold Every kingdom will hear how Oldtown cheered. The conquest ends not when they kneel - but when they cheer.#!
Remember this day. So shall I.
A Seat for the Dragon

The war is over. Six kingdoms bow to one crown, and now every lord and merchant and septon in Westeros asks the same question of me: where shall that crown live?

Dragonstone is the seat of my fathers - a fortress no fleet has ever taken, raised by Valyrian hands in the old way, with the salt and the smoke in its very stones. It is strong, it is mine, and it is where my line began. But it stands on an island at the edge of my realm, and a king who rules from the edge of his realm will find that the middle forgets him.

Then there is the hill where I first came ashore, at the mouth of the Blackwater. The Aegonfort is timber and mud, and the town rising around it is younger than my reign - but it stands where the realm's roads and rivers meet. The smallfolk have already given the place a name. They call it King's Landing.

My court must sit somewhere. It is for me to choose.
My throne shall stand at King's Landing.
Dragonstone shall remain the seat of my rule.
Harren built his towers to last forever. Now they serve a dragon.
My court shall sit at Oldtown, the oldest and greatest of cities.
The Forging of the Iron Throne

The Seven Kingdoms are mine, and a conqueror must have a seat worthy of them. I have given a command: that every blade raised against me - the swords of fallen kings and broken lords, gathered from the Blackwater to the Trident and the very gates of Storm's End - be carried here and laid before me.

We heap them high beneath the open sky, and I bid Balerion breathe. The Black Dread's fire runs white-hot, hot enough to melt a thousand blades into one. For days the smiths labour, beating the twisted, half-melted steel into a single monstrous chair - jagged, barbed and cruel, sharp enough to bite a careless hand.

The realm is already calling it the #bold Iron Throne#!. It is no comfortable seat, and I would not have it so. A king should never sit easy.
A king should never sit easy.
The Dragon rules over Westeros

The hall is full today, and the world outside it has changed.

My sisters stand at my sides, as they have stood since Dragonstone - Visenya at my right hand, Dark Sister at her hip even here; Rhaenys at my left, whose smile no man in this hall begrudges her. Below the throne the great lords of Westeros stretch back to the doors, and where once each of them looked to a different crown, now every eye in the realm turns to a single seat of fused and blackened steel.

I think of it as a single land now, and it is a strange thing to hold in the mind. From the Wall in its cold to the red mountains of the south, one law, one peace, one king. The rivers that men bled over for a thousand years run through one realm. The roads run unbroken. A merchant may ride from White Harbor to the Arbor and never cross a border under arms. What a hundred kings could not do in a hundred lifetimes, three dragons have done in a handful of years.

The maesters may keep their ledgers of which kingdom bent first and which was hardest to bring low. Those are small accountings, and they will be forgotten. This is what will be remembered: that the sky over Westeros belongs to House Targaryen, and shall belong to us for a thousand years and a thousand more. Long after my bones are dust and my sisters' names are songs, men will look up and know whose blood rules them. They will call us the House of the Dragon, and they will be right to.

And yet the land is not wholly one. South of the marches the sands lie quiet, and an old blind woman sits in Sunspear who told my sister that Dorne has no king to bend the knee, and sent my threats back to me unopened. Hers is the one banner in all of Westeros that has never dipped before my dragons.

#bold The realm is very nearly whole. Only Dorne stands apart - and whether it stands so for a season or for all time is mine to decide.#!
We did warn Princess Meria that we would return with Fire and Blood.
Dorne shall remain Unbowed, Unbent, Unbroken.
The Peace of the Dragon

The conquest is done, and the realm must now be taught to live with it.

From the Wall to the Dornish marches, the banners of the conquered kings are struck or sworn. Save only for the sun-scorched lords of Dorne, who keep to their sands and their spite, every great house of Westeros now bends to [ROOT.Char.GetFirstName].

No longer is [ROOT.Char.GetFirstName] merely the Lord of Dragonstone, nor a conqueror with a half-forged crown. From this day [ROOT.Char.GetFirstName] is #bold King of the Andals, the Rhoynar and the First Men, Lord of the Seven Kingdoms and Protector of the Realm#!.

And with the realm made one, one law above all others is proclaimed to every corner of it: the #bold King's Peace#!. From this day, no lord great or small - whatever his rank, whatever his grievance - shall make war upon his neighbor or settle his disputes with fire and steel. The private wars that bled Westeros for a thousand years are ended; justice belongs to the king's law, the king's courts, and the king's peace. Those who break it will answer to the Iron Throne - and the Iron Throne has dragons.

The lords will feast and swear their oaths anew. The dragon has brought peace to a land that knew only war - and, for now, the realm is one.
The Seven Kingdoms are almost one.

Six kingdoms kneel; the seventh hides behind its sands. The Yellow Toad told my sister that Dorne has no king to conquer — and promised us peril if we returned.\n\nWe warned her what our answer would be. Fire and Blood.

A Lyseni trader is ushered into my war council beneath a cloud of perfume, sea-salt, and expensive confidence. His wagons, he claims, carry engines built around immense torsion arms: scorpions capable of hurling iron bolts high enough to threaten even a dragon in flight.\n\nThe merchant makes no promise that his engines will slay Balerion. Buy the scorpions. Dragons bleed too.

Aegon Targaryen has sent his demand to Storm's End. I am to lay down the crown of Durran Godsgrief, bend my knee, and hold the stormlands by his leave. In return, the heathen promises that my house, my lands, and my lords will be spared. If I refuse, his armies will come south and his dragon with them.

He speaks as though the matter were already settled. Perhaps every lord who has knelt before him has taught him to expect obedience. He will find no such lesson here. My fathers held these lands against ironborn, Dornishmen, Andals, and every other enemy the gods saw fit to send against them. Storm's End has stood through a thousand years of war, and I did not wear Durran's crown this long to surrender it because a Valyrian boy arrived with a beast and called himself king.

Yet it is not only my crown that will burn if I choose wrongly. Every man who rides beneath the crowned stag has a wife, a son, a hall, or a field behind him. The Seven know I have never been called craven, but there are deaths a king may command for honor and deaths he commands only for pride.

Aegon will have his answer.

#bold If I bend, men may call me craven. If I do not, no man will ever dare it.#!

The dragonlord demands the Rock's allegiance and the crown of the Westerlands. Submission would preserve my house beneath his new order; refusal means trusting gold, stone, and western steel against dragonfire. Aegon's victories do not make this choice for me.

Aegon Targaryen demands that Dorne bow with the other kingdoms. He promises peace beneath his rule and fire for every holdfast that resists. Yet deserts have swallowed greater hosts than his, and a dragon cannot burn what it cannot find. I must answer.

The war for the Crownlands is over. Aegon Targaryen's banners stand above the roads and rivers I could not hold, and the Black Dread circles a realm that must now answer to the dragonlord. Whether by defeat or by my own submission, the issue has been settled, and my banners must come down.

Harren's Kingdom Broken

The war for the Kingdom of the Isles and the Rivers is finished. The Trident answers to the dragon now, the longships have been dragged home, and the crown Harwyn Hoare took by force has been taken back the same way.\n\nHarrenhal was raised so that no army of men could ever bring this house down. Against men the walls were answer enough. They were never an answer for this.

Forty years I spent on these stones. Forty years of ironborn sweat and riverland gold, and every mason who thought the work too slow was set to some slower work still. When the last tower went up I was the mightiest lord in Westeros, and I had the walls to prove it.

The dragonlord never threw them down. He did not need to. He took the rivers, and the isles, and the men who were meant to hold them, and left me the castle.

Harrenhal stands. My kingdom does not.

I have yielded, and there will be songs about it, and not one of them kind.

Forty years I spent raising Harrenhal so that no army raised by man could ever take it from me. The dragonlord did not bring an army of men. He offered me my life and the isles my fathers held, and asked only for the crown — and a crown is a smaller thing than a man's own bones burned black in his own hall.

The Kingdom of the Isles and the Rivers is ended. I am not.
The kingdom is lost. The walls are not.

Against all expectation, Aegon Targaryen has forced Dorne to yield. [fab_ac_news_a.GetShortUINamePossessive] resistance is ended, and the southernmost kingdom now stands beneath the Iron Throne. If even the deserts could not halt the dragons, every unconquered ruler must weigh what remains of hope.
Even Dorne has bent.
The Dragon Turned Back

The last of Aegon Targaryen's banners has withdrawn from [ROOT.Char.GetPrimaryTitle.GetNameNoTier]. What the dragonlord proclaimed an inevitable conquest has broken against our armies, our strongholds, and the resolve of those who refused to kneel.

His dragons brought terror from the sky, but they could not occupy every road, guard every camp, or compel a kingdom to surrender after its people chose resistance. The conqueror departs with fewer soldiers and a legend diminished by defeat. Across Westeros, rulers who had begun to regard Aegon's triumph as destiny will hear a different tale now.

[ROOT.Char.GetHouse.GetName] stood before fire and blood—and endured. The dragon can be resisted. The dragon can be beaten.
Send word of this victory to every kingdom.
Fire and Blood
I will spare my people. We submit.
We will meet fire with steel.

Faithful
