The Faith teaches that one god reveals seven faces: Father, Mother, Warrior, Maiden, Smith, Crone, and Stranger. Its worship is ordered through septs, septons, and the authority of the High Septon, with the Seven-Pointed Star at the heart of doctrine and devotion.
The Dragon's Right Hand
First Blood
The first army raised against the dragons burned in a single afternoon, and Westeros has taken note.
Bloodied in the Reeds
The fighting on the Gods Eye shore was won, and the ranks it thinned will be slow to fill again.
The Wailing Willows
A night raid out of the water gutted the baggage train and the rear guard. Replacements are slow in coming, and what is left costs more to keep in the field.
Dragonsbane
On a flooded field, in a storm that kept Meraxes on the ground, [CHARACTER.GetShortUINameNoTooltipNoFormat] rode forty horse at the dragon and drove a spear through her throat.
the Storm Queen
Proclaimed on the walls of Storm's End in her dead father's crown, with Orys's host below and Meraxes across the bay.
The Dragon's Envoy

The dragonlord's envoy stands before me in the great hall with Aegon's answer, and I make him give it before my lords. I offered Aegon Targaryen my daughter's hand and, as her dowry, the lands east of the Gods Eye between the Trident and the Blackwater, country the Storm Kings once held and Harren Hoare holds now. In return I asked for Dragonstone beside me when the time came to settle with Harren. There was sense in it. If Aegon wanted land, Harren had more than enough to lose, and I have never lacked the stomach to take it from him.

Aegon refuses the marriage. He has two wives already, both his sisters, and the heathen says he has no need of a third. Instead he offers his half-brother, Orys Waters, for Argella. The envoy calls him Aegon's companion and captain, as though command could put a father at a bastard's wedding or give him a name worth carving above a gate. Orys is baseborn, and Aegon proposes to put him in my daughter's bed.

That is not all. Aegon accepts the lands I named only as the beginning of the dowry. He also wants Massey's Hook and the Stormlander country running south from the Blackwater toward the Wendwater and the headwaters of the Mander. Those lands are mine already, held by men who have sworn before gods and men to Storm's End. I offered him Harren's hide, and the dragon has answered by reaching for mine.

There are men in this hall who would have the envoy thrown from the cliffs for less, and I do not blame them. Still, wrath is a poor reason to leave an enemy's meaning half heard. I will know the whole of Aegon's insolence before I decide what answer it deserves.
Guards. Take his hands. They are the only hands Aegon gets.
Say the whole of it. What else does the dragon offer?
Carry my refusal to Dragonstone. I have heard enough.
The Terms of the Bastard

I let the envoy finish. Orys Waters is to wed Argella, and the lands east of the Gods Eye that I first named will pass with the marriage if we take them from Harren. Aegon also demands Massey's Hook and the country between the Blackwater, the Wendwater, and the upper Mander. In return, Dragonstone joins me against Harren Hoare. Aegon's strength will be turned north, not south, and neither king is asked to swear to the other.

That last part saves the offer from the privy. There is no demand for homage in Aegon's letter, no tribute, and no claim upon Storm's End. He wants land, a marriage, and a common war, and for all his heathen ways he has at least remembered that he is writing to a crowned king rather than summoning some petty lord to his hall.

Orys remains the difficulty. Argella is my only heir, and the man she marries will stand closer to Storm's End than any outsider has a right to stand. Yet the Seven did not decree that a wife's house must vanish into her husband's merely because scribes find the custom convenient. If Orys enters this house through Argella, then he enters it on my terms. The child who succeeds her can bear the name Durrandon, inherit Durrandon blood through his mother, and sit the seat his mother's fathers held before Dragonstone was more than a smoking rock.

Aegon may have the lands he asked for and the marriage he proposed. I will have his strength against Harren, and Storm's End will remain in my blood and under my name. If that is not enough for him, then he never wanted an alliance at all. #bold Orys Waters may marry my daughter, but the heir to Storm's End will be a Durrandon.#!
He weds into my house or not at all. Send that word.
No. A thousand years of Durrandons do not end in this hall.
A Raven to Dragonstone

The raven leaves Storm's End before dusk. I write the answer myself, because the matter is simple enough to fit in one line and important enough that I will not have a maester polish the edge off it.

#italic Your brother is welcome. His sons will be Durrandons.#!

My lords have objections, and none of them are shy about giving voice to them. Some object to Orys's birth, some to the lands Aegon has demanded, and some to any compact with a man who beds his own sisters and calls it marriage. I have heard them all. The Seven may judge Aegon's soul when they please; I am concerned with Harren Hoare, three dragons, and whether House Durrandon still sits Storm's End when the fighting is done.

I have conceded land rather than fight Harren and Dragonstone together, but I have conceded neither my crown nor my house. If Aegon accepts the condition, Orys comes south as Argella's husband and the pact stands. If he refuses it, he may keep his bastard and learn what the stormlands cost by another road. #bold The terms are sent. Dragonstone may take them or choke on them.#!
We will have Aegon's answer soon enough.
The Dragon Answers

The answer from Dragonstone comes sooner than I expected, and Aegon accepts the condition without argument. Orys will come to Storm's End for the marriage, which will be made before my court and beneath the eyes of the Seven, and the children born to Argella will bear the Durrandon name and inherit through her.

The rest of the letter concerns the lands and the war. Massey's Hook and the country south of the Blackwater are to pass as agreed. When our banners move against Harren Hoare, Dragonstone will move with us. Aegon writes that he has no quarrel with a house that keeps faith with him and no wish to pull down an ancient line merely to prove that he can. Fine words from a man with three dragons, but I have heard worse terms from men with far less behind them.

I had expected haggling over the one condition I would not yield. Instead Aegon has accepted it at once, which means either that he understands the value of House Durrandon or that he is confident enough to let me keep my name while he takes what else he wants. I will discover which soon enough. #bold I asked for an ally against Harren. I have one, and I mean to see whether the dragon keeps faith as well as he writes it.#!
Open the gates to him. Storm's End fears no one bastard.
No. I will not marry my heir to Dragonstone after all.
A Wedding at Storm's End

They wed in the great hall beneath Durran's roof, before the Seven, the assembled storm lords, and enough witnesses that no man will later pretend he misunderstood the bargain. The septon names Argella Durrandon and Orys Waters before the Father and Mother, joins their hands, and calls upon the Seven to witness the vows. Aegon may make what excuses he pleases for wedding sister to brother on Dragonstone. In Storm's End, my daughter is wed according to the laws of gods and men.

Orys is not what some of my lords expected from a bastard of Dragonstone. He is broad, quiet, and careful with his courtesies. Men test him during the feast, as men will, and he gives none of them the quarrel they are looking for. I would almost prefer that he did, because a man's temper is easier to judge than his patience, but he repeats the terms of the marriage before the hall without hesitation. Argella's inheritance is hers, and the children who inherit through her will be Durrandons of Storm's End.

Argella has watched him closely since his arrival and has found more to say to him than she has said to me about the match. I will not call a handful of conversations affection, nor do I require it. Kings have married for poorer reasons than land, blood, and a useful sword, and many have done worse than a husband their daughter can bear to speak with. The marriage is lawful, the succession is settled, and the Seven have heard the vows. #bold Orys has entered House Durrandon. House Durrandon has not entered his.#!
Ours is the Fury, and no marriage changes that.
Pour the wine. The day has earned it.
The Storm Rides North

The marriage settled one half of the bargain. Harren Hoare is the other. His monstrous castle rises beside the Gods Eye, and the riverlands he rules lie between my kingdom and the lands I promised to Argella's marriage. If those lands are ever to change hands, Harren must first be torn out of them, and I have wanted that ironborn blackguard humbled since long before Aegon Targaryen learned to look west.

The storm lords gather and ride north by the old roads through the kingswood and toward the Blackwater. Orys rides with them, and Aegon's banners are already moving from Dragonstone. I have no intention of wasting good stormland men against Harrenhal's walls if dragonfire can answer stone more cheaply, but castles are not kingdoms. Harren has riverlords, crossings, granaries, ferries, and armies that must be held while the dragons earn the land I have paid for.

So the storm rides with the dragon against the ironborn. I would have preferred a son of proper birth at my daughter's side and a smaller price for the alliance, but the bargain has been sworn and I keep my oaths, whatever liberties Aegon takes with the laws of gods and men in his own bed. #bold Sound the muster. Harren has sat on stolen lands long enough.#!
The storm rides north. Harren stole from us first.
Send my lords. A king need not ride every road himself.
An Ally on My Border

Aegon Targaryen has come ashore at the mouth of the Blackwater, on the three hills where the fisherfolk beach their boats, and for the first time in my life a foreign host has landed within a few days' ride of my border without a stormlander reaching for a sword.

Massey's Hook is his. So is the country running south toward the Wendwater. I signed those lands away with my own hand and my own seal, which is a thing I have done for no man before, and there is no pretending they were taken from me. The lords who held them under Storm's End have new oaths to swear, and not one of them has sent me a complaint I would care to read aloud.

Riders came to these walls a year ago with word that dragons had been seen over the water, and men reached for their swords. Riders came again this morning with the same word, and it means the opposite. The beasts fly north once the muster is done. Harren Hoare spent forty years raising walls against an enemy worthy of them, and he will not wait much longer for one.

#bold The bargain is made. Now let the dragon prove he is worth what I paid for him.#!
The dragon is mine now. Harren will be the first to learn it.
The Price of Peace

The war has changed Westeros. Harren's grip on the riverlands is broken, and Aegon's ambitions have not ended with him. Reports from beyond my borders bring battles, bargains, submissions, and refusals, but none of them alters the agreement made here. The stormlands remain outside Aegon's rule, bound to him by marriage and treaty but not by oath, and I have no intention of allowing success elsewhere to make him forget the difference.

Aegon comes to Storm's End to speak of what follows. He confirms before I ask that Argella's children remain Durrandons and that the lands and rights already settled between us will stand. Then the heathen who once took care to write to me as one king to another asks for the one thing he left untouched.

He wants my crown. I am to surrender the kingship and remain Lord of Storm's End, with the stormlands, my vassals, my revenues, and my heirs left in my hands. I would rule the same country from the same seat, but beneath Aegon's crown instead of my own. Durran Godsgrief defied the gods themselves for this rock, and Aegon Targaryen now asks me to hand over what storms, ironmen, Andals, and Dornishmen all failed to take.

I know what war against his house would mean. I have seen the dragons at work, and only a fool mistakes knowing the strength of an enemy for fearing him. The question is whether I spend the lives of my lords and their sons to keep a circlet on my brow, or give Aegon his title and keep everything beneath it. #bold If I bend, it will be because I chose what House Durrandon could afford to lose, not because the heathen frightened me into it.#!
The crown is metal. Storm's End is stone, blood, and men.
Durran bent to no god. I will not bend to a heathen.
The Storm Bends, Unbroken

It is done in my own hall, before my own lords, because if I am to put down Durran's crown I will do it where every storm lord can see that no sword is at my throat. I place it in Aegon's hands myself. He receives it without triumph, sets it aside, and names me Lord of Storm's End, confirming the stormlands to me and my heirs beneath his crown.

Then my lords swear again. Yesterday their oaths ended with me. Today they pass through me to Aegon, but the men, castles, rents, judgments, and levies of the stormlands remain under the same hand. Argella is still my heir, and her children will still be Durrandons of Storm's End. Aegon has won a king's oath, not the right to unmake a thousand years of my house.

I was a king when the septon broke his fast this morning and I am not one now. I will not pretend that loss is nothing, nor will I grovel over it. Harren lost his lands, his line, and perhaps more besides. I have lost a crown and kept Storm's End, my daughter, my name, and every lord who mattered yesterday. Men may decide for themselves which bargain they would rather have made. #bold The crown is Aegon's. The storm remains Durrandon.#!
Ours is the Fury. King or lord, that much is mine.
The Envoy Rides Home Whole

I gave the envoy his answer before he had finished the offering of it, and I gave it standing, so that no man in the hall could mistake it for a thing still open to argument. Argella is not for sale to a bastard. Not for Harren's lands, not for Harren's head, and not for the friendship of a man who beds his own sisters and expects the Seven to look elsewhere.

Half my lords wanted him carried out in pieces. Fell said so plainly and Grandison said it louder. He went out through the gate on his own feet with his own hands, and that was not mercy. A king who cuts up heralds is a king no one troubles to send heralds to, and I have too many borders to spend that coin on one Valyrian's messenger. Aegon can have the refusal clean. He will not be able to tell it as the raving of an old man in a temper.

He will come south. I have expected it since the first raven flew to Dragonstone, and expecting it changes nothing. Ironborn, Andals, Dornishmen: every one of them came to this coast with better cause than a wedding refused, and every one of them went home short of men.

#bold He keeps his hands. He keeps his bastard. The rest we will settle in the field.#!
Send him home whole. The war comes either way.
The Whole of It, and No

I heard the whole of it. Every league of land, every clause, every courtesy. No homage asked, no tribute, no claim laid on Storm's End, and Dragonstone's strength turned north against Harren Hoare beside my own. I will not pretend it was a poor offer. It is better than any king in Westeros has been given by that family, and likely better than any will be.

It comes down to Argella all the same. She is my only child and the whole of my house after me, and Aegon proposes to settle her on a man with no name of his own and call the account balanced. A king may trade land. Land can be taken back, and I have taken some of it back twice in my life. What passes through a daughter passes once, and whatever is put in her bed sits in Durran's seat forever after.

So the answer is no, given whole and given knowing. No man will say afterward that I refused in anger without understanding what lay on the table. I understood it well enough. That is precisely why I would not have it.

#bold The dragon named a fair price. He asked for the one thing that was never for sale.#!
I have heard it all, and my answer stands.
The Raven Recalled

Eleven days I have had Aegon's letter, and eleven days I have read it and set it down and taken it up again. He granted the condition without a word of argument. Argella's children will be Durrandons, he writes, as though it cost him nothing. I named that condition because I was certain it would break the whole business, and a man does not surrender so easily the thing he means to keep.

Either he does not care whose name is cut above the gate so long as the gate is his, or he means to have that too and reckons it can wait a generation. I have sat across a table from men who conceded everything and took it all back before the ink dried. I have been one of them.

The envoy is long gone and there is nobody left in this hall to shout at but my own lords, who told me what they thought when the first raven flew. So a second raven goes tonight and it takes the offer back. Aegon will have been generous where all Westeros could see it and refused where all Westeros could see that, and the tale will be told that way in every hall from here to the Wall. And so it will be told. I would sooner be called changeable than be called the king who put a bastard's line in Durran's seat and thanked him for the favour.

#bold I asked a price I thought he would not pay. He paid it, and that is what decided me.#!
Send the raven. The offer is withdrawn.
The Goodson's War

Aegon has declared for my crown, and there is no dressing this as an invasion. His brother sat at my table two winters ago and swore before the Seven that his sons would carry my name. The men marching out of Storm's End marched beside those banners at the Gods Eye. Some of them buried friends from that host and will now go looking for the ones who lived.

He wants the circlet and nothing beside it. Not Storm's End, not the stormlands, not Argella's inheritance. He has asked for none of them and he will get none of them by asking. Only the crown of Durran Godsgrief, and only because a realm with two kings in it is not yet the realm he says he has.

Orys will come south. Aegon has sent Orys for the stormlands from the beginning and sees no reason to stop now. My own goodson against my own banners, and whatever grandsons the gods see fit to give me will hear about it from whichever side is left to do the telling.

#bold I kept every oath I swore to that house. I never swore them this one.#!
Call the banners. The crown was never his to ask for.
He is my daughter's husband. He will swear it.
Send him back to his brother.
Take him. He'll not command my men.
The Goodson's Oath

I have him brought into the great hall with every storm lord in Storm's End standing to watch it, because a thing done quietly is a thing that can be argued about later. Orys Waters is my daughter's husband, my grandsons will carry my name, and his brother's host is marching down my roads. Two of those three are worth something to me. I mean to find out which.

He does not make me ask twice. He goes down on one knee on the stones in front of the whole hall, and he says it plainly and without ornament: that he is sworn to Storm's End and to the house he married into, that Aegon released him of nothing when he sent him south, and that he will draw his sword for me against any man living. He does not say his brother's name. I notice that he does not, and I let it pass.

Argella watches from the dais and does not look at me once. She has more to lose here than either of us and she knows exactly what I would have done to him if he had hesitated. He did not hesitate. Whatever else the Seven made him, they did not make him a coward, and I have known a great many highborn men who were.

So he rides with us. Men will say I was a fool to allow it and those men are welcome to say so where I can hear them. I have taken oaths from better-born men who kept them worse.

#bold He knelt in my hall and swore before the Seven. Now let the dragon come and see what he bought with that bastard.#!
Rise, goodson. You ride on my right hand.
The Hook Comes Home

The terms are signed and I keep the crown. Aegon has not lost his realm and I will insult neither of us by claiming he has. He has lost a war he chose to begin, and he has paid for it in the only coin I wanted.

Massey's Hook is Durrandon ground again. So is the Wendwater forest and the woods along the Baywater, which means every holding south of that new town of his sends its levies to Storm's End now. The Storm Kings held all of it before a Targaryen ever crossed the water, and I have held it twice in one lifetime, which is more than most men manage with anything.

There is less satisfaction in it than I expected. Orys is still my goodson and Argella is still his wife, and there are storm lords in the ground who rode under the dragon's banners before they rode against them. A war won is a war won. It is not the same thing as never having needed one.

#bold He came for the crown of Durran Godsgrief and went home with less than he brought.#!
The Hook answers to Storm's End again.
The Price Paid Twice

The terms Aegon sets are the terms he set before a single man died. My crown for my lands. Storm's End, the stormlands, my lords, my revenues, and Argella after me, all of it kept and all of it held beneath his. Not one word has moved. He did not need to move it.

So I have bought with a war exactly what I was offered for nothing, and all I have to show for the difference is the certainty that I could not have won it. I told my lords I would not be frightened into kneeling, and I was not. I was beaten into it. The singers may find that prettier. I do not.

The worst of it is not Aegon. Aegon is a conqueror and conquerors take crowns, and there is no great shame in losing to a man who has taken six of them. The worst of it is that his brother sits at my table on feast days, wed to my daughter, and that the men who broke my host will be drinking in my hall before the year is out.

#bold I would not sell the crown. In the end I gave it away and paid for the privilege.#!
Take it, then. It cost me a war to learn its price.
The Muster of the Storm

So it is war. I have rejected Dragonstone and called my banners, and the storm lords have answered as storm lords should. Fell comes from Felwood, Errol from Haystack Hall, Buckler from Bronzegate, Grandison from Grandview, and Dondarrion down from Blackhaven with every marcher sword he can spare. Aegon may call himself whatever he pleases on his rock. South of the Blackwater, men still answer to Argilac Durrandon.

The rains have come early and hard. Roads that were firm a fortnight ago are mud from the Blackwater south, and every stream is running high. The Seven have sent me weather fit for a Storm King. A dragon can cross country that would stop an army, but Orys still needs wagons, fodder, dry bowstrings, and ground on which men can stand.

Orys is marching south with the greater part of Aegon's host, and Rhaenys Targaryen is with him on Meraxes. I have more men, better knowledge of the country, and lords defending their own fields. He has a dragon. I do not need to pretend that last advantage is small, but neither will I behave as though one beast has already conquered the stormlands. Where we meet will decide whether Orys learns that himself.
The kingswood. He will learn what my trees conceal.
The open field. No hedges, no tricks, no excuses.
The Rainwood. Orys can drown in it first.
Rain on the Kingswood

Fell, Buckler, and Errol struck the Targaryen van as it crossed the Wendwater. They came out of the trees at first light, killed men before Orys could bring the rest of his host into order, and withdrew before the weight of his army could close around them. By midday a great many of his men were dead or missing, and the storm lords had disappeared back into country they have hunted, ridden, and bled over since boyhood.

Rhaenys brought Meraxes up before midday, but low cloud, driving rain, and the tree cover kept her from finding the raiders in force. She burned stretches of woodland along the road and forced the storm lords farther back, but most had already scattered before the dragon reached them. I am told some of Orys's men cheered when she came overhead. Men cheer loudly when they need reminding that they are not afraid.

The ambush has cost Orys blood and time, and it has shown us how quickly Meraxes can punish a mistake. Good. I would rather know the beast's reach now than discover it with half my host trapped beneath her. #bold Orys has entered my country. He will pay for every road, ford, and stand of trees he takes from me.#!
Keep cutting. Give the bastard no peaceful mile.
Enough small fighting. Draw him toward a battle line.
The Wroth King

News of the fighting has travelled beyond the stormlands. Merchants and envoys bring questions about the Wendwater and about Meraxes being checked by the weather. The rest of Westeros can gossip. The only judgment that concerns me is inside my own camp, where men who once looked skyward at every shadow have now seen dragon men bleed like any others.

My lords have watched Orys lose men on roads he does not know. They have watched Meraxes forced low by rain and wind. Their confidence has returned, and I mean to use it before caution grows back into fear. A lord may be forgiven for respecting a dragon. He will not be forgiven for teaching his men to fear one before it appears.

Orys still has a disciplined host, and Rhaenys still has Meraxes. I know that as well as any trembling maester who can add one dragon to one army and declare the sum unbeatable. #bold We have bloodied them once. By the Warrior, I mean to do it again before they remember their courage.#!
Ride with the van. I will not shelter behind my lords.
Hold the line. Prudence is not fear.
Wings Pinned

The gale has settled over the coast and has not eased for three days. Meraxes remains on the ground above the Wendwater with her wings folded tight against the rain. My scouts have seen Rhaenys try to take her up twice, and both attempts ended almost as soon as they began. If the Seven mean to hand me a dragon chained by weather, I will not insult them by refusing the gift.

Without Meraxes in the air, Orys has to move as any other commander does. His host is smaller than mine, deep in country that answers to Storm's End, and forced onto roads the rain has reduced to mud. He may be Aegon's Hand, brother, bastard, or all three together. On the ground he is still a man leading men, and I have beaten better men than him.

The weather will not hold forever. When the wind drops, Rhaenys will rise again and every advantage changes with her. Until then the field belongs to soldiers, and no one south of the Blackwater has more right to it than I do. #bold While Meraxes is grounded, Orys will learn what became of every man who mistook the stormlands for easy country.#!
March. The Warrior has given us our hour.
Send scouts. I want to know whether men could reach her.
The Sky Turns Black

The wind eased before dawn, and Rhaenys wasted no time. Meraxes took the air low over the trees and found the storm lords who had been troubling Orys's march since the Wendwater. The rain had soaked the forest for days, but dragonfire burned through wet leaves, green branches, horses, and men alike. The Stranger took his due quickly once she found them.

Lord Errol is dead. Fell and Buckler brought back what they could of their commands, many without shields or horses, and every man among them reeks of smoke. They speak less of the men they lost than of the sound Meraxes made above the trees before the fire came down. I will not call them cravens for it. A craven runs before the danger arrives. These men stood until the sky itself burned them out.

I can replace horses. I cannot replace lords, and I will not keep feeding good men into woods that Meraxes can turn into a furnace merely to prove I possess courage. Anyone who mistakes prudence for fear may say so in my hearing. #bold The dragon is flying again. We change the war before she changes it for us.#!
Scatter the host. The beast can hunt shadows.
Hold together. Every bow we have will be waiting for her.
The Lords Waver

Three lords came to my tent tonight, and none of them came only for himself. Grandison spoke for the rest. Errol is dead, Fell has lost near half the men he took north, Buckler is short of horses, and every raven from the coast brings another account of villages emptying before the Targaryen advance. No man in the tent used the word fear. They are storm lords, and they have earned better than that from me.

Then Grandison told me Aegon's terms are being repeated openly through Orys's camp. Any storm lord who bends the knee keeps his lands, his castle, and his name. The heathen has learned enough of Westeros to know where to place the knife. He is not asking my lords to betray their homes. He is offering to spare those homes if they betray me.

Grandison did not ask leave to desert. He said that if I commanded him to remain, his house would remain and take whatever came with it. By the Seven, that is why the decision is mine rather than his. Their oaths give me the right to demand everything. A king who spends brave men merely because they are brave enough to obey him has mistaken pride for duty. #bold I will decide what loyalty to House Durrandon requires, and no dragonlord will decide it for me.#!
Hold them to their oaths. None leaves while I stand.
Cravens and oathbreakers. They can run home to their walls.
Bronzegate Broken

Bronzegate is taken, my army has been forced back across the Slayne, and I have perhaps eleven thousand men left of the twenty thousand who answered the first muster. The right gave way at the ford after Meraxes made repeated passes over it. Those men were not cravens. I saw horses burning beneath them and men trying to close ranks while their shields caught fire. The Warrior himself could ask no more of mortal men. Buckler died holding them together long enough for the rest to cross.

The road to Storm's End lies open behind me. I have sent Argella back with orders to prepare the castle and keep the garrison steady. She knows as well as I do that walls alone will not win this war while Meraxes can fly, but Storm's End has outlived every fool who thought stone was all that held it.

I still have an army, and Orys has not destroyed it. If I continue yielding ground, there will soon be no ground left between him and my daughter's inheritance. Like Aegon and Maegor

Judgment upon Five

This Old Man

Braxton stands before the throne in polished armor, his arrogance untouched by chains. “Then I choose trial by combat. We meet in full armor with our shields up. He carries a morningstar and all the strength of nineteen years. Honor the trial. Then Saera goes to Oldtown.

Gently. She is not to be frightened.
